extracted.subtask_description: Practical craft guidance for writing screenplays: designing image systems, titling, and a staged method (step-outline → treatment → screenplay) emphasizing inside-out development and rigorous testing. Includes principles for symbolism, pitching, and disciplined revision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Image System must be subliminal
rubrics_metrics.description: An Image System is a repeated set of motifs/images that works beneath consciousness to shape meaning; it must be subliminal so the audience is unaware of it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repeat an image (e.g., water in LES DIABOLIQUE) so it seeps into the audience's unconscious; avoid making the audience recognize the pattern as 'symbolic'—recognition turns the symbol into a neutral intellectual curiosity and robs it of power. Use repetition with variation; the symbol should bypass cognition as music or scoring does. Example anti-patterns: the hamhanded, declamatory symbolism in remakes like CAPE FEAR, BRAM STOKER’S DRACULA, and THE PIANO which label symbols and flatten emotional impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Image System: kinds and use (internal vs external; linking/separating; archetypal progression)
rubrics_metrics.description: Image Systems can be external (environmental motifs) or internal (psychic/psychological motifs); they can link or separate characters and build from particular to archetypal meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design multiple Image Systems if needed (e.g., CASABLANCA uses imprisonment motifs, archetypal progression linking Rick to America, and linking/separating imagery between characters). Use compositions and repeated objects (windows, blinds, mirrors, eyes) to express internal states (e.g., CHINATOWN's 'blind seeing'). Combine opposing external systems (water vs drought) to heighten irony or theme. Vary images and compositions across scenes to sustain and deepen meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who authors the Image System
rubrics_metrics.description: The screenwriter should begin the film’s Image System; the director and designers finish and realize it on screen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writer originates the ground of imagery in the script since they envision the story’s physical and social world; as writing proceeds, patterns of imagery often emerge in descriptions and dialogue. If no Image System arises, invent one and quietly embroider it into the story. Be aware that while directors are ultimately responsible for every shot, few understand the difference between decorative and expressive photography—so a clear writer-originated Image System helps secure expressive imagery in production.

rubrics_metrics.name: Titles should position and point to story elements
rubrics_metrics.description: A film’s title is a marketing centerpiece that prepares/positions the audience; an effective title points to something solid in the story—character, setting, theme, or genre.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Best titles often name two or more elements (e.g., JAWS = character + wild setting + theme; KRAMER VS. KRAMER = characters + divorce theme; STAR WARS = epic conflict/genre). Avoid 'nontitle' literary titles that don't indicate story content (e.g., TESTAMENT without reference, LOOKS AND SMILES that fails to position). Titles are part of marketing—consider audience positioning and commercial realities (Harry Cohn anecdote). Use the working title MOMENT BY MOMENT until you find a title that truly points to the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer inside-out writing method over outside-in
rubrics_metrics.description: Successful writers typically work inside-out: develop story design thoroughly before drafting the screenplay; the struggling writer often works outside-in by writing scenes and clinging to favorite set pieces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inside-out means spending months on step-outlines and treatments, generating and discarding material until the best story survives. Outside-in writers invent scenes, get attached to favorites, force fits, and produce a screenplay that 'sucks' despite good scenes. The inside-out approach yields consistent quality, dependable production of work, and better long-term growth; outside-in tends to burn out the writer and results in scripts that read well on craft but fail structurally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step-outline standard
rubrics_metrics.description: A step-outline tells the story in one- or two-sentence steps, each describing what happens in a scene and noting on the back of the card which structural step (Inciting Incident, First Act Climax, Mid-Act Climax, etc.) that scene fulfills.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use stacks of 3x5 cards (one stack per act) and keep them months if necessary. On the back of each card indicate the scene’s role in the story design (e.g., which step it sets up). Be brutal: create far more material than you keep and discard until only the best steps remain. A proper step-outline lets you pitch the story coherently and allows structural changes without wasting draft pages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pitch test requirement (ten-minute pitch rule and reaction criteria)
rubrics_metrics.description: Before treatment, pitch the step-outline to intelligent listeners; the story must hook, hold, and pay off within a ten-minute pitch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Watch listener behavior: are they hooked by the Inciting Incident, leaning in, and held through turns? On reaching the Climax does the listener react (a whispered 'Wow') and fall silent—silence indicating deep emotional/esthetic engagement? If a good majority of listeners do not respond with enthusiasm, do not proceed; 'enthusiasm' means sustained engagement and emotional payoff, not over-the-top reactions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment standards (what a treatment should be)
rubrics_metrics.description: A treatment expands the step-outline into paragraph-by-paragraph, moment-by-moment present-tense description of each scene, underlaid with full subtext, but without dialogue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treatments for a feature commonly reach 60–90 double-spaced pages when fully expanded (studio-era treatments were 200–300 pages). Modern ten- to twelve-page 'treatments' are often inadequate. Use the treatment to discover how scenes actually play, to flesh subtext (conscious and unconscious thoughts/feelings), and to rework, cut, add, or reorder scenes while preserving the proven overall design from the step-outline. Only after treatment is solid should you move to screenplay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Screenplay drafting rules (when and how to write the screenplay)
rubrics_metrics.description: Convert the finished treatment into screenplay, adding dialogue after the treatment stage; dialogue written at this point tends to be the finest because characters have been fully prepared by prior stages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When converting, translate treatment description to screen description and add dialogue; expect first drafts to still need revisions, and when dialogue reveals structural faults, return to the treatment to fix setups and payoffs rather than tinker superficially. Writing from a thorough treatment can allow screenwriting at a clip of 5–10 pages per day; avoid short-cutting the treatment stage because premature screenplay drafting produces a 'surrogate treatment' that is narrow and underexplored.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delay writing dialogue until after treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: Prematurely writing dialogue (outside-in) chokes creativity because it encourages attachment to spoken words and halts exploration of events and character as actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dialogue is the most visible output and therefore easy to overvalue; writing it too early makes writers loath to cut speeches even when the underlying dramatic events or story turns require change. Place 'tape over their mouths' until after treatment so characters' voices emerge naturally and distinctly when dialogue is finally written.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create copious material and destroy ruthlessly
rubrics_metrics.description: In the search for quality, produce far more material than you intend to use and be willing to discard large amounts until only the best remains.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept that roughly 90% of your ideas will be mediocre; sketch scenes dozens of ways and throw out those that fail. Keep research, biographies, images, vocabulary snippets in files while letting the story itself remain disciplined in the step-outline. This method increases the chance of discovering 'gem-quality' story material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symbolism anti-pattern: do not label symbols
rubrics_metrics.description: Labeling or declaiming a symbol destroys its unconscious power; overtly symbolic images flatter critics and render symbols inert.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid obvious, repeated signposting that tells the audience 'this is symbolic.' Reasons some filmmakers do this include flattering an elite intellectual audience or attempting to influence critics; both are artistic compromises. Use subtlety—let the repetition and variation carry meaning without conscious recognition.
